# Kingu: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Kingu** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**Tiāmat Makes Kingu Her Consort.** The epic's first tablets set the stage in catastrophe.  Apsû, the primordial freshwater, cannot sleep for the noise of the young gods and plots to destroy them; Ea preempts him, wraps Apsû in sleep, and kills him, building his own sanctuary on the still waters (Enuma Elish I).  Tiāmat, the salt sea, endures this in silence — until her own offspring drive her to fury.

**The Tablet of Destinies.** To legitimate Kingu's command, Tiāmat performs the epic's most consequential gesture short of battle: she fastens the Tablet of Destinies — the ṭuppi šīmāti, the inscribed register by which fates are decreed and confirmed — upon his breast.  To hold the tablet is to hold the power to bind and loose the destinies of gods and worlds; Kingu is thus briefly made a rival sovereign, and the younger gods are thrown into terror, because fate itself seems to have defected to chaos.  In Mesopotamian thought the tablet was no metaphor: legitimate kingship meant the gods' confirmation of a ruler's decrees, and its seizure marks every true transfer of power in the mythic record — as the Anzu poem shows when the lion-headed bird steals the same authority from Enlil.

**Marduk Defeats Kingu.** The divine assembly, helpless, offers kingship to any god who can answer the threat — and Marduk of Babylon answers, on a chilling condition: 'When I speak, let my word be confirmed; the command I utter, let the gods fulfill it' (Enuma Elish III).  The gods test him by destroying a garment and commanding him to restore it; he does, and they arm him with the flood-weapon and the storm-wind.  In single combat Marduk splits Tiāmat with an arrow, fashions heaven and earth from her body, and then turns to her army.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves


## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Kingu
- **ASCII form:** kingu
- **Meaning:** "Unknown"
- **Domain of influence:** Dragon, Consort of Tiamat
- **Pantheon:** Mesopotamian
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒆥𒄖
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 260 of 546

## The Name Travels

Kingu is a specifically Babylonian figure, but his narrative pattern — the defeated dragon whose body becomes the stuff of human life — echoes across the Near East and beyond. The closest parallel is Tiāmat herself: where she becomes the physical cosmos, Kingu becomes the biological substrate of humanity.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Kingu** stands at [/kingu/](/kingu/) — [lore](/kingu/lore/), [scholars](/kingu/scholars/), [patterns](/kingu/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.

## The Sources Are Open

The myths above are retold from the temple's record; the primary voices are in the [Sacred Texts](/texts/): [Enūma Eliš](/texts/enuma-elish/) and [The Epic of Gilgamesh](/texts/gilgamesh/). Nothing in this file outranks them.
